questions.question: LeetCode 206 Reverse Linked List: what are the time and space complexities of this iterative solution?
options: O(n) time, O(n) space
O(n log n) time, O(1) space
O(n) time, O(1) space
O(n^2) time, O(1) space
questions.explanation: Every node is visited exactly once and only three reused pointers are held, so the pass is linear in time with constant extra space.

questions.question: Which technique finds the middle of a singly linked list in a single pass without knowing its length?
options: Fast and slow pointers
Binary search over node indices
Copying the nodes into a TreeMap
Reversing the list, then walking halfway
questions.explanation: A fast pointer moving two steps for each single step of the slow pointer reaches the end exactly when the slow pointer reaches the middle.

questions.question: Merge Two Sorted Lists: why do the cleanest solutions start with a dummy head node?
options: It makes the merge stable for equal values
It removes the need to special-case the first result node
It halves the number of value comparisons
It lets the merge finish in O(log n) time
questions.explanation: The dummy guarantees an existing predecessor, so appending the very first node needs no separate branch and dummy.next is the final head.

questions.question: Linked List Cycle I: Floyd's tortoise and hare beats the HashSet approach mainly in which respect?
options: Worst-case time drops to O(log n)
It also reports the cycle length for free
Extra space drops from O(n) to O(1)
It works only on doubly linked lists
questions.explanation: Both run in O(n) time, but the two-pointer method keeps only two references while a HashSet may store up to n node references.

questions.question: Remove Nth Node From End: which edge case explains why a dummy node before head is recommended?
options: n equals the list length, so the head itself is removed
The list contains duplicate values
n is larger than the list length
The list length happens to be even
questions.explanation: When n equals the length, the node to delete is the head; a dummy predecessor lets the identical unlink statement handle that case.

questions.question: Add Two Numbers stores digits in reverse order. Why does that ordering simplify the solution?
options: It lets you use recursion instead of iteration
It guarantees both lists have equal length
Least significant digits sit at the heads, matching carry flow
It removes the need for a dummy head node
questions.explanation: Addition propagates carries from the least significant digit upward, and reverse storage puts those digits first so one forward pass suffices.

questions.question: In Java, which java.util.LinkedList operation runs in O(1) worst case?
options: get(int index)
contains(Object o)
indexOf(Object o)
addFirst(E e)
questions.explanation: LinkedList keeps head and tail references, so addFirst only relinks two nodes; indexed access and searching must walk the chain.

questions.question: Linked List Cycle II: after the pointers meet, why does walking one from head and one from the meeting point reach the cycle start?
options: The meeting point is always the node just before the start
Head-to-start equals meeting-to-start, modulo the cycle length
The fast pointer has looped exactly twice by the meeting point
The meeting point is always halfway around the cycle
questions.explanation: From 2(F+a) = F+a+kC you get F = kC-a, so F steps from head and F steps from the meeting point both land on the cycle entrance.

questions.question: Palindrome Linked List in O(1) extra space: which sequence of steps is the standard approach?
options: Push every value on a Deque, then pop and compare
Sort the list, then compare it with the original
Recursively compare node i with node n-1-i
Find the middle, reverse the second half, compare halves
questions.explanation: Reversing only the second half in place lets two pointers compare the halves; the Deque and recursive variants both cost O(n) extra space.

questions.question: Intersection of Two Linked Lists: why does this loop terminate when the lists never intersect?
options: Both pointers hit null on the same step, so a == b ends it
The shorter list is exhausted first and the method returns
An internal counter caps the loop at m + n iterations
The pointers meet at the tail node of the longer list
questions.explanation: Each pointer walks A then B (or B then A), covering identical total distance, so they arrive at null together and the equality test exits.

questions.question: Copy List with Random Pointer in O(1) extra space: what does the node-interleaving trick do first?
options: Stores every original node in a HashMap keyed by value
Inserts each copied node directly after its original
Reverses the list so random pointers point forward
Sorts the nodes by their random pointer targets
questions.explanation: With each copy woven in behind its original, copy.random is just original.random.next, found in O(1); the two lists are unzipped afterwards.

questions.question: Reorder List turns L0..Ln into L0, Ln, L1, Ln-1, ... Which plan achieves O(n) time and O(1) space?
options: Sort the list, split it, then merge the halves
Copy nodes into an ArrayList and rebuild with two indices
Reverse the whole list, then merge it with the original
Find the middle, reverse the second half, merge alternately
questions.explanation: Splitting at the middle, reversing the tail half in place, then weaving the two halves produces the required order without extra storage.

questions.question: This Odd Even Linked List solution groups nodes by index. What does it return for 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5?
questions.explanation: Odd-position nodes keep their relative order and the even-position chain is appended unchanged, giving 1,3,5 followed by 2,4.

questions.question: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II deletes every duplicated value. Why is a dummy node essential here but not in problem 83?
options: Problem 82 must also keep the result sorted
Problem 82 needs O(1) space while 83 does not
The head itself may be a duplicate and must be removed
Problem 82 has to traverse the list twice
questions.explanation: In 83 the first occurrence always survives, but in 82 a duplicated head is deleted, so a dummy predecessor is needed to relink the new head.

questions.question: Rotate List: which step in this solution prevents wasted work when k is far larger than the list length?
options: Reversing the list k separate times
Reducing k with k %= n before rotating
Returning head unchanged whenever k > n
Breaking the temporary cycle at newTail
questions.explanation: Rotating by n restores the original list, so only k mod n matters; that reduction also turns k = 0 into an immediate return.

questions.question: Partition List must keep the original relative order inside each partition. Which approach guarantees that?
options: Swapping node values whenever an out-of-place pair appears
Sorting the list and then splitting it at x
Running quickselect with x as the pivot
Building two dummy-headed lists, then joining them
questions.explanation: Appending nodes in traversal order to a less-than list and a greater-or-equal list preserves relative order, and joining them is O(1).

questions.question: Swap Nodes in Pairs solved recursively as shown: what are its time and space costs?
options: O(n) time, O(n) space from the recursion stack
O(n) time, O(1) space
O(n log n) time, O(log n) space
O(n^2) time, O(n) space
questions.explanation: Each node is touched once, but the recursion nests n/2 frames deep, so the call stack costs O(n); the iterative version is O(1) space.

questions.question: Merge k Sorted Lists with a heap of size k over N total nodes: what is the overall time complexity?
options: O(N k)
O(k log N)
O(N log k)
O(N log N)
questions.explanation: Each of the N nodes is pushed and popped exactly once from a heap holding at most k entries, so every node costs O(log k).

questions.question: Sort List runs in O(n log n). What extra space does the usual top-down merge sort on a linked list use?
options: O(n) for an auxiliary array
O(1), genuinely constant
O(n log n)
O(log n) for the recursion stack
questions.explanation: Splitting and merging only relink existing nodes, so no array is allocated, but the recursion nests about log n frames deep.

questions.question: Cycle detection: F = nodes before the cycle, a = steps from cycle start to meeting point, C = cycle length. Which relation holds?
options: F = kC - a for some integer k >= 1
F = a + C
F = C - 2a
a = F + C
questions.explanation: The hare covers 2(F+a) and the tortoise F+a, and their difference is a whole number of loops, so F + a = kC, giving F = kC - a.

questions.question: This iterative Reverse Linked List attempt loops correctly. What does it return for 1 -> 2 -> 3?
options: The single node 1, with nothing after it
null
questions.explanation: The reversal itself is correct, but returning head yields the node that is now the tail, whose next was set to null, so only 1 is returned.

questions.question: In this LRU Cache, what breaks if the third argument to super() changes from true to false?
options: Eviction stops entirely and the map grows unbounded
get stops refreshing recency, so eviction becomes FIFO
put starts throwing ConcurrentModificationException
Lookups degrade from O(1) to O(n)
questions.explanation: accessOrder=true makes get move an entry to the end of the order; with false the map stays insertion-ordered, so the eldest entry is FIFO, not LRU.

questions.question: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List: besides splicing children in, what must an accepted solution also do?
options: Sort the flattened nodes by value
Return a deep copy of the flattened list
Null out every child pointer and repair all prev links
Keep child pointers so the structure can be rebuilt
questions.explanation: The result must be a proper flat doubly linked list, so every child field has to be null and each node's prev must point at its new predecessor.

questions.question: Merge k Sorted Lists: merging one list at a time into an accumulated result costs what, for N nodes across k lists?
options: O(N log k)
O(k N)
O(N log N)
O(N + k)
questions.explanation: The growing accumulator is re-traversed on every merge, so the k merges sum to about kN node visits; divide and conquer reduces this to O(N log k).

questions.question: Sort List in strictly O(1) extra space, excluding the input, is achievable with which variant?
options: Bottom-up merge sort with iterative sublist merging
Top-down merge sort relying on tail recursion
In-place quicksort over the linked nodes
Heapsort driven by a PriorityQueue of nodes
questions.explanation: Bottom-up merge sort merges sublists of size 1, 2, 4, ... inside a loop, so it needs neither recursion frames nor an auxiliary array.

questions.question: This Remove Nth Node From End attempt: what happens on 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 with n = 2?
options: It removes node 4, the correct answer
It removes node 3
It throws NullPointerException
It removes node 5, the last node
questions.explanation: fast must advance n+1 steps from the dummy; advancing only n leaves slow one node too far, so the tail is unlinked instead of node 4.
